description:
Building a working web application that takes SAR data and turns it into an easy-to-understand map of Earth-surface changes. Current: Radar/signal processing, OTFS/Doppler, AI/ML, Python, MATLAB.

Required: React, JavaScript/TypeScript, APIs, GIS/GDAL, GeoPandas, interactive maps, and deployment.
summary: Sindh Crop Pulse is an interactive website that uses NASA‑ISRO NISAR radar data to show a full farming season around Sukkur, Sindh, Pakistan. Because radar sees through clouds and works at night, it can track crops during the monsoon, when normal satellite photos are often blocked. Users can play a time‑lapse of five NISAR passes from June to October 2026, compare any two dates with a swipe view, and tap any spot to see how its vegetation changed. The app turns complex radar data into a simple picture that farmers, planners and students can understand.
details:
What it does: Sindh Crop Pulse is an interactive website that shows a full farming season around Sukkur, Sindh, Pakistan, using radar data from the NASA‑ISRO NISAR satellite. It maps about 100 × 100 km of farmland around Sukkur, Shikarpur and Larkana, coloured by a Radar Vegetation Index (RVI), from brown for bare soil to deep green for dense crops. Users can play a time‑lapse of five NISAR passes (17 Jun, 23 Jul, 28 Aug, 3 Oct and 27 Oct 2026), compare any two dates with a swipe divider, and tap any spot to see that field’s own season curve. A short explainer shows how radar sees crops.

How it works: We searched ASF Vertex for NISAR Level‑2 GCOV products and kept only Track 41, Frame 15 ascending passes, so every image views the area from the same angle. We downloaded the data with Google Colab and the asf_search library. In Python we read the L‑band HH and HV layers, cut out our area, and averaged 10 × 10 pixels (10 m to 100 m) to reduce speckle. We calculated RVI = 4·HV / (HH + HV), and marked pixels darker than –18 dB as water or no signal, because noise there gives a false high RVI. The results go into a small JSON file that the website draws in the browser.

Benefits and impact: The monsoon crop season is exactly when clouds block normal satellite photos. Radar works through clouds and at night, so it can follow crops when other satellites can’t. Pakistan’s food security depends on the Indus plain, and a tool like this could help track planting and harvest timing, spot fields that fail to grow, and help students and the public understand radar data. We found that on 3 October the lowest RVI values dropped sharply (10th percentile from about 0.3 to 0.14), matching the rice season, when rice standing in water creates a strong radar “double bounce.”

Tools: Python (h5py, NumPy, pyproj, Matplotlib, asf_search), Google Colab, Google Drive, NASA Earthdata and ASF Vertex, HTML, CSS, JavaScript, VS Code and Netlify. No special hardware.

Creativity: Instead of showing raw grey radar images, the app tells the story of a season as a time‑lapse anyone can play, and it explains the physics behind the colours, such as why flooded rice looks bright in HH radar.

Factors we considered: comparing only images from the same track and frame; radar noise over water giving false vegetation values; keeping the website small and fast enough to work on a phone; and being honest about limits. We only have five passes, there’s no ground-truth crop map yet, and the whole-area average is diluted by desert and towns. Next steps are adding all 11 passes, a farmland-only average, and grouping fields by their seasonal pattern to tell rice from other crops.
